title: Four hundred years of the Granth
word: Four hundred years of the Granth
hook: Sikhs mark four centuries since the Granth was first installed at the Harmandir
tomorrow: Three hundred years of the Guru Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa's anniversary, and your line was three hundred years. Which beginning did you celebrate? Today the count goes back further, to a book carried into a shrine. Day one thousand twenty-three.

The crowd steps aside for a book. It is wrapped in cloth and carried on someone's head, and behind it walks a man waving a chaur, the whisk of honor, the way you would for a king. At the end of the walk is a shrine standing in a pool, and inside it a raised seat waiting. Tradition remembers this as the day the Granth was first set in place at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Centuries later, Sikhs counted back to that day and filled the same walkways. Today: four hundred years of the Granth.
screen: `A BOOK CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `A WHISK OF HONOR.` → `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Tradition says Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and included the words of saints from other backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim, whose hymns sang of the One. Bhai Gurdas wrote the volume down as the Guru dictated. Second, the installation. The volume was carried into the Harmandir Sahib and opened there, and tradition says Baba Buddha was appointed to read from it. Third, the seat. The story Sikhs tell is that Guru Arjan had the book placed on a high seat, and he himself sat lower. The living Guru sat beneath the book he had compiled. That small arrangement says something large: the Word comes first, and even the Guru bows to it. Fourth, the seal. Near the close of the volume comes a short passage known as the Mundavani, at Ang 1429. In it, Guru Arjan says that on this platter three things have been placed: truth, contentment, and contemplation. Anyone who eats from it, he says, is saved. A feast, set out for whoever comes. When Sikhs marked four hundred years, they were not only honoring an old book. They were remembering the day the platter was first set on the table, and noticing that it's still there, open, every morning. That's today's line: four hundred years.
screen: `GURU ARJAN GATHERS THE HYMNS.` · `CARRIED INTO THE HARMANDIR.` · `THE GURU SITS LOWER.` · `TRUTH, CONTENTMENT, CONTEMPLATION.` · then, large: `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes at the open page. If you have a gutka, or a page of gurbani on your phone, open it now, to any page, without choosing. If you don't, simply picture a book lying open on a cloth. Breathe in, and let your eyes rest on one line, or on the picture. Breathe out, and set three things on an imagined platter in front of you: truth, contentment, contemplation. Sit with them, one breath each, and then all three together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly between them. The bell holds the time.
Four hundred years of the Granth. The anniversary of the day, tradition says, the volume compiled by Guru Arjan was installed at the Harmandir Sahib, with the Guru seated below it. Today's word.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS OF THE GRANTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: four hundred years. Today, read one page of the Granth, in a gurdwara, a gutka or online, and carry one line with you until evening. Day one thousand twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 1023 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE GURU GRANTH.`

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is carried with honor, placed on a raised seat under a canopy, and opened each morning; Sikhs mark the anniversary of its first installation at the Harmandir Sahib with kirtan and readings.

fork.setup: you're Guru Arjan, and the book you compiled is now installed in the shrine. where do you sit?
fork.reveal: the story Sikhs tell is that the Guru had the book placed high and sat beneath it: the Word first.

original.note: Mundavani, the seal: a short passage near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1429.

trapdoor: what you thought: the birthday of a holy book.
what it means: the anniversary of the volume Guru Arjan compiled being installed at the Harmandir Sahib.
what a scholar hears: a Guru who sat lower than the Word he gathered, a volume that welcomed saints from other backgrounds, and a seal, the Mundavani, that sets the meal out for anyone.

notes: The year in the index hook is left out under the claims rule; the count comes from the title. The hook line in this file was reworded without the year.
Please confirm Macauliffe vol. 3 supports: the compilation, Bhai Gurdas as scribe, Baba Buddha appointed to read, and Guru Arjan seated lower than the book.
'The fifth Guru' is a count given by standard Sikh tradition; confirm it is acceptable.
Mundavani at Ang 1429 paraphrased (thaal vich tin vastoo paeeo, sat santokh veechaaro); please confirm wording, including 'is saved'.
Original: ਮੁੰਦਾਵਣੀ; please confirm spelling and stress.
Editor pass: hook reopened ('The crowd steps aside for a book') so it no longer starts with the 'A [noun]...' scene pattern used by most nearby hooks; no factual changes.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): 'the volume ends with the Mundavani' was inaccurate as stated: in the standard bir the Raagmala follows it on Ang 1429-1430, and its place is debated, so the script now says the Mundavani comes near the close. The practice no longer invites listeners to open a full Granth at home (a saroop is kept with prakash and maryada); it offers a gutka or gurbani online, and the carry matches.
